## The question

[I keep failing to understand what I'm doing wrong - derivatives](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2968619/i-keep-failing-to-understand-what-im-doing-wrong-derivatives), asked by [Matthew](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/607788/matthew) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2018-10-24; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> I need to find the derivative of this function:
>
> $f(x)=x^2(x-2)^4$
>
> I have gone about this two ways:
>
> 1. Chain Rule inside a Power Rule
>
> $$f(x)=x^2(x-2)^4$$
> (I found the derivative of $(x-2)^4$ using the chain rule.)
> $$f'(x)=(x^2)(4)(x-2)^3(1)+(x-2)^4(2x)$$
> $$f'(x)=4x^2(x-2)^3+2x(x-2)^4$$
>
> 2. Power Rule only
>
> $$f(x)=x^2(x-2)^4$$
> $$f'(x)=(x^2)(4(x-2)^3)+(x-2)^4(2x)$$
> $$f'(x)=4x^2(x-2)^3+2x(x-2)^4$$
>
> My calculator gives me the same answer that I get in method 2. However the textbook says the answer to this problem is $2x(x-2)^3(3x-2)$
>
> So, assuming the textbook is correct (it better be), what are my calculator and I doing wrong? Also, why does the using the chain rule inside of the power rule produce a different result? I only ask the second question because I was under the impression that the chain rule was just another shortcut for finding derivatives.
:::

Both terms in $4x^2(x-2)^3+2x(x-2)^4$ are multiples of $2x$ and $(x-2)^3$.  So factor them out:
$$4x^2(x-2)^3+2x(x-2)^4 = 2x(x-2)^3[2x+(x-2)] = 2x(x-2)^3(3x-2)$$
